newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanians cool to return of exiled king.
newsitem.headline: Albanians cool to return of exiled king.

text.p: President Sali Berisha says he is open to a royalist proposal for a referendum on reverting to a monarchy, but most Albanians believe the return of their exiled king would do little to resolve the country's conflict.

During talks on Sunday which produced an agreement to form a national unity government and hold fresh elections by June, a small monarchist party proposed including a plebiscite on the form of government.
This might allow the return of King Leka I, although many Albanians believe a royal comeback is still a remote possibility, even given the present turmoil in the country.

His reception would be uncertain. Another Balkan monarch, King Michael of Romania, returned to adoring crowds in 1992. But when he came back a second time this month, his citizenship restored, he was greeted by disappointingly small groups.
Leka Zogu, 57, who lives in South Africa, was only a few days old when he fled Albania with his father King Zog in 1939 as Italian dictator Benito Mussolini sent troops to occupy the country.
He says he is willing to return to help to guide the affairs of state but opposes the armed insurrection now gripping Albania.
"As far as I know no other party is opposed to such a referendum," Guri Durollari of the monarchist Legality Movement told a meeting of Albania's 10 political parties, broadcast on state television.

Berisha said the issue could be considered at a future meeting. "This is too far apart from the issues we are now discussing. We cannot include it in a statement. But you can raise it on television," he said.

The prospect of a restored monarchy drew mixed reactions on the streets of Tirana. Some people thought a king might help drag the country out of crisis while others were more sceptical and suggested he should return as a private citizen.
"It would be good to have him back," said 29-year-old Beni. "He's not mixed up with all the dirty mess here."
Arjan, another young man, agreed, saying: "Let him come. That would at least be a positive moral act."
But Marika, a 40-year-old woman, was not keen. "We don't need the king any more than we need the politicians. We've had enough, enough of all of them," she said.

Luljeta, also in her 40s, was similarly dismissive of the king over the water. "He is no one of any importance in political or economic terms," she said. "His father was a king, but as for him, let him come as a normal citizen and stay out of politics."

Leka, tall and bespectacled, tried to visit Albania in 1993, saying he recognised the legitimacy of republican rule. He was unceremoniously bundled back onto a private aircraft within 24 hours on the grounds that his passport marked "Kingdom of Albania" was invalid.
Last month, he called on the government to resign over its handling of a series of collapsed pyramid investment schemes which left hundreds of thousands of Albanians penniless.
"All the reports I am getting from Albania at this moment are that the only person they have any interest in is me," he told Reuters in South Africa.
Leka, who would like to see the creation of a "Greater Albania" taling in Albanian regions in Kosovo and Greece, was proclaimed king when his father died in Britain in 1961.
